title: दसैँ : बुबाको ४० हजारदेखि खर्बौँको आर्थिक परिचालनसम्म
content:
यसपालि दसैँ मनाउन म आफ्नो गाउँ गुल्मी आएको छु । संयोगले पाँच वर्षदेखि दसैँ मनाउन पाएको थिइनँ । अघिल्लो महिना मात्रै नेपाल आएर फर्किएको थिएँ । फेरि यति चाँडै आउने योजना थिएन। तर एक दिन बुबाको फोन आयो । म घरको जेठो छोरा हुँ, तैपनि बुबाले मायाले सधैँ ‘कान्छा’ भन्नुहुन्छ। फोनमा पनि उही आत्मीय स्वर सुनियो, ‘कान्छा, यो दसैँमा त आइज है। अनि सुन् न, आउँदा ४० हजार जति पैसा साटेर ल्याएस् है ।’ बुबाले त्यति भनेपछि मनले मानेन । टिकट काटेँ, पैसा साटेँ र दसैँ मनाउन गुल्मीको घर आएँ । घरमा अर्को कुरा थाहा भयो । बुबाले घरमै पालेका दुई वटा खसी प्रतिगोटा ४० हजार रुपैयाँका दरले बेच्नुभएछ । दुई वटा खसीबाट ८० हजार रुपैयाँ आयो । मैले ल्याएको ४० हजार जोड्दा एउटै परिवारसँग सम्बन्धित एक लाख २० हजार रुपैयाँको आर्थिक प्रवाह देखियो । त्यो सबै दसैँमा खर्च भएको रकम होइन, तर पैसा कसरी एक घरबाट अर्को घर र गाउँको बजारसम्म पुग्छ भन्ने उदाहरण हो । त्यसपछि सोचेँ दसैँमा हाम्रो घरमा मात्रै यति रकम चलायमान भयो भने देशभरिका लाखौँ घरमा कति रकम घुम्दो हो ? दसैँ टीका, जमरा र पारिवारिक मिलनको पर्व हो । तर यसले गाउँको गोठ, बजारको पसल, यातायात, बैंक, उद्योग र विदेशमा कमाइरहेका नेपालीलाई एउटै आर्थिक सम्बन्धमा जोड्छ। यसलाई केवल खर्च गर्ने पर्व भनेर बुझ्दा यसको ठूलो आर्थिक पक्ष छुट्छ । बुबाले बेच्नुभएको ४० हजारको खसी कसैले किनेर घरमा लग्यो । आफन्त जम्मा भएर मासु खाए । त्यो रकम बुबाको हातमा आयो । उहाँले त्यही पैसाले नातिनातिनालाई लुगा किन्नुभयो भने कपडा पसलेको व्यापार बढ्यो । पसलेले थोक व्यापारीलाई पैसा तिर्‍यो । थोक व्यापारीले सामान ढुवानी गर्ने गाडीलाई भाडा दियो । चालकले घरमा खाद्यान्न किन्यो । बुबाले केही रकम बैंकमा राख्नुभयो भने त्यो निक्षेपमार्फत वित्तीय प्रणालीमा पनि परिचालन हुन सक्छ। एउटै खसीको पैसा कति ठाउँमा पुग्यो ! खसी गाउँबाट काठमाडौँ आएको भए अझ धेरै हात जोडिन्थे। किसान, सङ्कलनकर्ता, ट्रक चालक, सहचालक, बजारका मजदुर, मासु पसले र अन्तिम उपभोक्ता । किसानले ३० हजारमा बेचेको खसी सहरमा ४० हजारमा बिक्री भयो भने बीचको १० हजार सबै व्यापारीको नाफा होइन, ढुवानी, मजदुरी, हेरचाह र जोखिमको खर्च पनि त्यहीँबाट जान्छ । पशु सेवा क्षेत्रका अधिकारीलाई उद्धृत गरिएका सार्वजनिक विवरणमा दसैँका बेला देशभर करिब १० लाख खसी बोका बिक्री हुने अनुमान उल्लेख भएको छ। यसलाई औसत प्रतिगोटा २५ हजारदेखि ४० हजार रुपैयाँको मूल्यमा राखेर हेर्दा २५ देखि ४० अर्ब रुपैयाँको सम्भावित कारोबार देखिन्छ । यो बिक्रीको अन्तिम सरकारी हिसाब होइन, बजारको परिमाण बुझाउने अनुमान हो । काठमाडौँ उपत्यकामा मात्रै विभिन्न वर्षमा दसैँको आसपास दशौं हजार खसी बोका र च्याङ्ग्रा भित्रिएका विवरण छन् । मुस्ताङको च्याङ्ग्रा, कर्णालीको खसी, तराईको माछा र गाउँघरका कुखुरासम्म यसै मौसममा बजार पाउँछन् । दसैँमा खसी मात्र बिक्री हुँदैन । चामल, चिउरा, तेल, मसला, तरकारी, फलफूल, मिठाई, दूध र पेय पदार्थको माग बढ्छ । कसैले आफ्नै घरको खसी काट्छ, कसैले छिमेकीसँग मिलेर किन्छ । गाउँको पैसा गाउँमै अर्को घरमा पुग्छ । उधारो उठ्छ, बाँकी ज्याला तिरिन्छ, पसलमा रोकिएको हिसाब मिल्छ । बैंकको डिजिटल कारोबारमा नदेखिएका यस्ता साना नगद लेनदेन पनि आर्थिक जीवनका वास्तविक गतिविधि हुन् । गाउँको एउटा सानो बजार सम्झौँ । दसैँको अघिल्लो दिन किसानले खसी बेचेर ३५ हजार रुपैयाँ ल्यायो। उसले किराना पसलको पुरानो उधारो तिर्‍यो । किराना पसलेले थोक व्यापारीलाई बाँकी रकम बुझायो । त्यही पसलमा काम गर्ने युवाले पारिश्रमिक पाएपछि घरमा चामल र नयाँ कपडा लगे। उता खसी किनेको परिवारले मासु काट्ने व्यक्तिलाई ज्याला दियो, मसला र तरकारी किन्यो। यहाँ रकमको प्रत्येक हस्तान्तरण नयाँ आम्दानी होइन । तर एक अर्कासँग गाँसिएका धेरै परिवारको दैनिक जीवनलाई यसले सहज बनायो । नयाँ लुगा लगाउने परम्पराले कपडा, जुत्ता, सिलाइ, झोला, गहना र घरायसी सामानको बजार चलाउँछ । एउटा परिवारले पाँच जनाका लागि कपडा किन्दा त्यसको प्रभाव पसलदेखि थोक व्यापारी र ढुवानीसम्म पुग्छ। सामान चीन वा भारतबाट आएको रहेछ भने रकमको एउटा हिस्सा विदेशी उत्पादकसम्म पुग्छ । सन् २०२५ मा चाडपर्व लक्षित करिब ३५ अर्ब रुपैयाँ मूल्यका आयातित सामान सीमा अवरोधमा रोकिएको व्यापारीहरूको विवरणले पनि दसैँको बजार अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय आपूर्ति शृङ्खलासँग जोडिएको देखाउँछ । नेपाली ढाका, अल्लो, गार्मेन्ट, जुत्ता र घरेलु उत्पादनको हिस्सा बढाउन सके यही मागले देशभित्र थप रोजगारी दिन सक्छ । यातायातलाई हेरौँ । काठमाडौँमा काम गर्ने मानिस रोल्पा फर्किन्छ, पोखराको विद्यार्थी झापा जान्छ, विदेशबाट आएको छोरा विमानस्थलबाट गाउँ पुग्छ । बस मालिकले भाडा पाउँछ; चालक, सहचालक, इन्धन पम्प, बाटोको चिया पसल, होटेल र मिस्त्रीको पनि काम बढ्छ । घर फर्किने मानिसले आमाबुबाका लागि उपहार, छोराछोरीका लागि कपडा र घरका लागि सामान लिएर जान्छ । सहरमा कमाएको पैसा गाउँतर्फ बग्छ। घर रङ्गरोगन गर्दा पेन्टर, सिकर्मी, हार्डवेयर पसल र मजदुरको आम्दानी जोडिन्छ । दसैँको यात्राले सहरमा मात्र होइन, बाटोछेउका बस्तीमा पनि कारोबार बढाउँछ । बिहानैदेखि चिया पकाउने होटेल, खाना खुवाउने भोजनालय, पेट्रोल पम्प, टायर मर्मत गर्ने ग्यारेज र साना फलफूल पसलले ग्राहक पाउँछन् । एउटा बसमा चढेका चालीस यात्रुले फरक फरक ठाउँमा गरेको सानो खर्च जोड्दा पनि धेरै परिवारसम्म पैसा पुग्छ । तर अत्यधिक भाडा, भिडभाड र सडक दुर्घटनाको जोखिम कम गर्नसके मात्र यस्तो आवागमन सुरक्षित र फलदायी हुन्छ । विदेशमा रहेका नेपालीका लागि दसैँको अर्को अर्थ छ । कोही बिदा मिलाएर फर्किन्छन्, कोही टिकट महँगो भएर वा काम छाड्न नसकेर आउँदैनन् । फर्किन नसक्नेले पनि घरमा पैसा पठाउँछन् । विदेशको कमाइ आमाको हातमा पुग्छ, त्यो पैसा गाउँको किराना पसल, किसान र यातायात व्यवसायीसम्म पुग्छ । नेपालमा आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ मा करिब २३ खर्ब ६३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ रेमिटेन्स भित्रिएको प्रकाशित तथ्याङ्क छ। यसको मासिक औसत झन्डै १ खर्ब ९७ अर्ब हुन्छ। त्यो सबै दसैँमा खर्च हुने होइन, तर चाडपर्वको पारिवारिक खर्च धान्ने एउटा महत्त्वपूर्ण स्रोत रेमिटेन्स हो । विदेशबाट दसैँ मनाउन आउने मानिसको खर्चमा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय हवाई टिकट पनि जोडिन्छ । केही रकम विदेशी विमान कम्पनी र सेवा प्रदायककहाँ पुग्छ, केही नेपालका विमानस्थल, यातायात, होटेल र स्थानीय व्यवसायमा खर्च हुन्छ । फर्किन नसकेका नेपालीले घरमा पठाएको रकमले पनि बजार चलाउँछ । नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकको २०८२/८३ को वार्षिक विवरणअनुसार रेमिटेन्स करिब २३ खर्ब ६३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ पुगेको थियो। यो वर्षभरि आएको रकम हो, दसैँमा मात्रै आएको होइन। तथापि चाडपर्वको बेला विदेशको कमाइले परिवारको खर्च धान्न गर्ने सहयोगलाई यो परिमाणले बुझ्न मद्दत गर्छ । सरकारी र निजी क्षेत्रका धेरै कर्मचारीले दसैँको आसपास चाडपर्व खर्च पाउँछन् । श्रम ऐनले श्रमिकका लागि वर्षमा एक पटक एक महिनाको आधारभूत पारिश्रमिक बराबर चाडपर्व खर्चको व्यवस्था गरेको छ । मानौँ, १० लाख कर्मचारीले औसत ३० हजार रुपैयाँ पाए भने एकै अवधिमा ३० अर्ब रुपैयाँ उनीहरूको हातमा पुग्छ । यो उदाहरणका लागि गरिएको गणना हो। कसैले लुगा किन्छ, कसैले टिकट काट्छ, कसैले उधारो तिर्छ । व्यवसायका लागि भने तलब र चाडपर्व खर्च एकै पटक व्यवस्थापन गर्नुपर्ने दबाब पनि हुन्छ । राष्ट्रिय जनगणना २०७८ अनुसार नेपालमा ६६ लाख ६६ हजार ९३७ घरपरिवार छन् । सबैले दसैँ मनाउँदैनन् र खर्च पनि समान हुँदैन। तैपनि प्रतिपरिवार औसत २० हजार रुपैयाँ खर्च भएको परिकल्पना गर्दा करिब १ खर्ब ३३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ हुन्छ । औसत ३० हजार भए करिब दुई खर्ब रुपैयाँ पुग्छ । यो दसैँको प्रमाणित कुल खर्च होइन, यसको सम्भावित आर्थिक आकार बुझाउने हिसाब हो। खसी बोका, कपडा र यातायातका छुट्टाछुट्टै रकम यसमा फेरि जोड्दा एउटै खर्च दोहोरिन सक्ने भएकाले सावधानी चाहिन्छ । दसैँमा बैंकमा पैसा जम्मा हुन्छ, खाताबाट नगद निकालिन्छ, मोबाइल र QR बाट भुक्तानी हुन्छ । तर गाउँघरमा खसी किनबेच, मजदुरी, उधारो फर्छ्योट र साना पसलका धेरै कारोबार नगदमै पनि हुन्छन् । बैंकमा जम्मा भएको वा डिजिटल माध्यमबाट गएको रकमले मात्रै आर्थिक गतिविधिको सम्पूर्ण तस्बिर दिँदैन । मानौँ, किसानले ५० हजारको खसी बेच्यो, २० हजारको लुगा र खाद्यान्न किन्यो, पसलेले कर्मचारीलाई तलब दियो, कर्मचारीले घर भाडा तिर्‍यो । एउटै पैसा विभिन्न हातमा पुग्यो । यसलाई मुद्राको चलन गतिसँग जोडेर बुझ्न सकिन्छ । तर पटक पटक भएको कारोबारलाई त्यति नै नयाँ राष्ट्रिय आय भनेर गन्न मिल्दैन । बैंकको खातामा देखिएको कारोबार र गाउँको हाताहाती नगद कारोबारलाई एउटै कुरा ठान्न हुँदैन । उदाहरणका लागि, आमाले घरमा राखेको बचतबाट नातिलाई दक्षिणा दिनुभयो, नातिले पुस्तक वा जुत्ता किन्यो र पसलेले आपूर्तिकर्तालाई भुक्तानी गर्‍यो । यसमध्ये केही कारोबार बैंकको अभिलेखमा तुरुन्त नदेखिए पनि वस्तु र सेवाको वास्तविक कारोबार भएको हुन्छ । त्यसैले दसैँको आर्थिक आकार नाप्दा नगद, डिजिटल भुक्तानी, बचत, उधारो र वस्तुको आफ्नै घरमा हुने उपभोगसमेत बुझ्नुपर्छ । भारतमा दीपावली, चीनमा नयाँ वर्ष, अमेरिकामा क्रिसमसको किनमेल सिजन र मुस्लिम बहुल देशहरूमा ईदले पनि यात्रा, व्यापार, होटेल, उपहार र सेवा क्षेत्रलाई चलायमान बनाउँछन् । भारतको व्यापारी सङ्गठनले सन् २०२५ को दीपावली सिजनमा वस्तु र सेवातर्फ करिब ६.०५ लाख करोड भारतीय रुपैयाँको कारोबार भएको अनुमान सार्वजनिक गरेको थियो । खेलकुदतर्फ विश्वकप फुटबल र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय क्रिकेट प्रतियोगिताले पर्यटन, प्रसारण, विज्ञापन र आतिथ्य क्षेत्रमा यस्तै माग सिर्जना गर्छन् । नेपालमा दसैँसँगै तिहार, छठ, ल्होसार, माघी, इन्द्रजात्रा र अन्य पर्वहरूको पनि आर्थिक प्रभाव अध्ययन गर्न सकिन्छ । यद्यपि दसैँ सबैका लागि सहज हुँदैन । कसैले व्यापार बढाउँछ, कसैले ऋण लिएर चाडपर्व मनाउँछ । महङ्गो टिकट, बढ्दो मूल्य र सामाजिक अपेक्षाले कम आम्दानी भएका परिवारलाई दबाब दिन्छ । त्यसैले दसैँको आर्थिक सफलता कति रकम खर्च भयो भन्नेमा मात्र होइन, त्यसले कति नेपाली किसान, श्रमिक र उद्यमीको आम्दानी बढायो भन्नेमा खोज्नुपर्छ । दसैँको व्यापार बढेको खबरसँगै अर्को प्रश्न पनि उठ्छ नाफा कसको हातमा पुग्यो ? मुस्ताङको पशु पालकले उचित मूल्य पाए कि पाएनन् ? कपडा पसलका कर्मचारीले समयमै तलब पाए कि पाएनन् ? यात्रुबाट बढी भाडा उठाइयो कि उचित सेवा दिइयो ? चाडपर्वको कारोबार बढ्नु मात्र पर्याप्त छैन, त्यसको लाभ उत्पादन गर्ने, बोक्ने, बेच्ने र किन्ने सबैबीच न्यायोचित रूपमा बाँडिनु पनि आवश्यक छ । नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंक, राष्ट्रिय तथ्याङ्क कार्यालय, भन्सार, पर्यटन क्षेत्र र निजी व्यवसायीले मिलेर दसैँको वास्तविक आर्थिक प्रभाव अध्ययन गर्न सके राम्रो हुन्थ्यो। कति खसी बोका बिक्री भए, कति रेमिटेन्स आयो, कति मानिसले यात्रा गरे, कति रकम स्वदेशी उत्पादनमा गयो, कति आयातमा खर्च भयो र कति रोजगारी सिर्जना भयो यस्ता प्रश्नको उत्तर चाहिन्छ । अन्त्यमा फेरि बुबाकै कुरा सम्झिन्छु। उहाँले दुई वटा खसी बेचेर ८० हजार रुपैयाँ पाउनुभयो । मैले ४० हजार रुपैयाँ साटेर ल्याएँ । तर त्यो एक लाख २० हजारको हिसाबभन्दा ठूलो कुरा उहाँको एउटा वाक्य थियो ‘कान्छा, यो दसैँमा त आइज है ।’ त्यही एउटा वाक्यले मलाई घर फर्कायो । कति नेपाली यस्तै बोलावटमा फर्किन्छन् होला, कति फर्किन नसकेर पैसा मात्र पठाउँछन् होला । दसैँको अर्थतन्त्र यही मानवीय सम्बन्धमा टिकेको छ । किसानको गोठ, मजदुरको ज्याला, चालकको स्टेयरिङ, व्यापारीको पसल र विदेशमा कमाउने छोराछोरीको बचत सबैलाई यसले कुनै न कुनै रूपमा जोड्छ । दसैँ नेपालको सांस्कृतिक पहिचान मात्र होइन, मुद्रा प्रवाह, उपभोग, व्यापार, रोजगारी र ग्रामीण–सहरी सम्बन्धलाई चलायमान बनाउने प्रमुख मौसमी मेरुदण्डमध्ये एक हो । हामीले कति खर्च गर्‍यौँ भन्दा पनि त्यो खर्चले कति नेपालीको हातमा आम्दानी पुर्‍यायो भन्ने प्रश्न महत्त्वपूर्ण छ । This time, I have come to my village Gulmi to celebrate Dashain. Coincidentally, I had not been able to celebrate Dashain for five years. I had only returned from Nepal last month. I had not planned to come back so soon. But one day, my father called me. I am the eldest son of the family, yet my father always affectionately calls me 'Kancha'. The same affectionate voice was heard on the phone, 'Kancha, come this Dashain. And listen, when you came, you brought 40,000 rupees in exchange.' When my father said that, I didn't agree. I bought a ticket, exchanged money, and came home to Gulmi to celebrate Dashain. I learned something else at home. My father had sold two goats he had raised at home for 40,000 rupees each. He earned 80,000 rupees from the two goats. When I added the 40,000 I brought, I saw a financial flow of 120,000 rupees belonging to the same family. That's not all the money spent on Dashain, but it's an example of how money reaches from one house to another and to the village market. Then I thought, if this much money circulates in our house alone during Dashain, how much money circulates in millions of homes across the country? Dashain is a festival of tika, jamara, and family reunions. But it also connects the village cowshed, market shops, transportation, banks, industries, and Nepalis earning abroad into a single economic relationship. Understanding it as a festival of spending only misses its huge economic aspect. Someone bought the goat that the father had sold for 40,000 and took it home. The relatives gathered and ate the meat. That money came into the father's hands. He used the same money to buy clothes for his grandchildren, and the business of the cloth shop grew. The shopkeeper paid the money to the wholesaler. The wholesaler rented a vehicle to transport the goods. The driver bought food for the house. If the father had put some money in the bank, that money could also be mobilized in the financial system through deposits. How many places could the money from a single goat have reached! If the goat had come from the village to Kathmandu, more hands would have been joined. Farmers, collectors, truck drivers, assistant drivers, market workers, butchers, and the final consumer. If a goat sold by a farmer for 30,000 is sold in the city for 40,000, the 10,000 in between is not only the profit of the trader, but also the cost of transportation, labor, care, and risk. Public statements quoted from livestock service officials indicate that around one million goats and sheep will be sold across the country during Dashain. If we put this at an average price of Rs 25,000 to Rs 40,000 per goat, a potential turnover of Rs 25 to 40 billion is seen. This is not the final government estimate of sales, but an estimate to indicate the size of the market. In the Kathmandu Valley alone, there are reports of tens of thousands of goats and sheep being imported around Dashain in various years. Mustang's Chyangra, Karnali's Khasi, Terai fish, and even village chickens find a market during this season. Not only is Khasi sold during Dashain. Demand for rice, Chiura, oil, spices, vegetables, fruits, sweets, milk, and beverages increases. Some slaughter their own goats, while others buy them together with their neighbors. Village money reaches other households in the village. Loans are taken out, wages are paid, and accounts held in shops are settled. Such small cash transactions that are not visible in the bank's digital transactions are also real activities of economic life. Let's think of a small market in the village. The day before Dashain, a farmer sold a goat and brought 35,000 rupees. He paid off the old loan from the grocery store. The grocery store paid the remaining amount to the wholesaler. After receiving his salary, the young man working in the same store took home rice and new clothes. On the other hand, the family that bought the goat paid the wages of the butcher, bought spices and vegetables. Here, each transfer of money is not new income. But it has made the daily life of many families who are closely connected to each other easier. The tradition of wearing new clothes drives the market for clothes, shoes, sewing, bags, jewelry, and household goods. When a family of five buys clothes, the impact extends from the store to the wholesaler and the transporter. If the goods come from China or India, a portion of the money goes to the foreign manufacturer. Traders’ accounts of about Rs 35 billion worth of imported goods targeted for the festival in 2025 being stopped at border barriers also show that the Dashain market is linked to the international supply chain. If the share of Nepali Dhaka, Allo, Garment, Shoes, and Home Products can be increased, this demand could create more jobs within the country. Let's look at transportation. A person working in Kathmandu returns to Rolpa, a student from Pokhara goes to Jhapa, a son who has come from abroad reaches his village from the airport. The bus owner gets the fare; the work of the driver, co-driver, fuel pump, roadside tea shop, hotel and mechanic also increases. People returning home take gifts for their parents, clothes for their children and household goods. The money earned in the city flows to the village. When a house is painted, the income of the painter, carpenter, hardware shop and laborer increases. Dashain travel not only increases business in the city but also in the roadside settlements. Hotels serving tea, restaurants serving food, petrol pumps, tire repair garages and small fruit shops get customers from the morning. Even if the small expenses of forty passengers on a bus are added up, the money reaches many families. But such travel is safe and fruitful only if the risk of high fares, congestion and road accidents can be reduced. For Nepalis living abroad, Dashain has another meaning. Some return after arranging a vacation, some do not come because the ticket is expensive or they cannot leave work. Even those who cannot return send money home. The earnings from abroad reach the hands of their mothers, and that money reaches the village grocery stores, farmers, and transport entrepreneurs. There is published data that about 2.363 trillion rupees in remittances entered Nepal in the fiscal year 2082/83. Its monthly average is about 1.97 trillion. Not all of that is spent on Dashain, but remittances are an important source of meeting family expenses during the festival. International airfares are also part of the expenses of people coming from abroad to celebrate Dashain. Some of the money goes to foreign airlines and service providers, while some is spent on Nepali airports, transportation, hotels, and local businesses. The market is also driven by the money sent home by Nepalis who are unable to return. According to the annual report of Nepal Rastra Bank for 2082/83, remittances reached about 2.363 trillion rupees. This is the amount received throughout the year, not just during Dashain. However, this amount helps to understand the contribution of foreign earnings to meet family expenses during the festival. Many government and private sector employees receive festive expenses around Dashain. The Labor Act has made a provision for festive expenses equal to one month's basic salary for workers once a year. Suppose, if one million employees receive an average of 30 thousand rupees, 30 billion rupees will reach their hands in the same period. This is a calculation done for example. Some buy clothes, some buy tickets, some pay off loans. For businesses, there is also pressure to manage salaries and festive expenses at the same time. According to the National Census 2078, there are 66,66,937 households in Nepal. Not everyone celebrates Dashain and the expenses are not the same. However, assuming an average expenditure of Rs 20,000 per household, it is about Rs 133 billion. If the average is Rs 30,000, it is about Rs 200 billion. This is not the verified total expenditure of Dashain, but an estimate of its potential economic size. Caution is required as the same expenditure may be repeated when separate amounts for goats, clothes and transportation are added to this. During Dashain, money is deposited in banks, cash is withdrawn from accounts, and payments are made through mobile and QR. But in rural areas, goat buying and selling, wages, loan repayments, and many small shop transactions are also done in cash. The amount deposited in banks or transferred through digital channels alone does not give the entire picture of economic activity. Suppose, a farmer sold a goat worth 50,000, bought clothes and food worth 20,000, a shopkeeper paid his employees' salaries, and an employee paid his house rent. The same money reached different hands. This can be understood by linking it to the movement of money. But repeated transactions cannot be counted as new national income. The transactions seen in the bank account and the cash transactions in the village should not be considered the same thing. For example, a mother gave dakshina to her grandson from the savings kept at home, the grandson bought books or shoes, and a shopkeeper paid a supplier. Some of these transactions, although not immediately visible in the bank's records, are actual transactions of goods and services. Therefore, when measuring the economic size of Dashain, cash, digital payments, savings, loans, and consumption of goods in one's own home should also be considered. Diwali in India, New Year in China, Christmas shopping season in the US and Eid in Muslim-majority countries also drive the travel, trade, hotel, gift and service sectors. The Confederation of Indian Industry had estimated that the turnover of goods and services during the Diwali season in 2025 was around 6.05 lakh crore Indian rupees. In sports, the World Cup football and international cricket tournaments create similar demand in the tourism, broadcasting, advertising and hospitality sectors. Along with Dashain in Nepal, the economic impact of Tihar, Chhath, Lhosar, Maghi, Indrajatra and other festivals can also be studied. However, Dashain is not easy for everyone. Some increase their business, some take out loans to celebrate the festival. Expensive tickets, rising prices, and social expectations put pressure on low-income families. Therefore, the economic success of Dashain should be seen not only in how much money was spent, but also in how many Nepali farmers, workers, and entrepreneurs it increased their income. With the news of increased Dashain business, another question arises: who gets the profit? Did the cattle breeders of Mustang get a fair price or not? Did the employees of the clothing store get their salaries on time or not? Were passengers overcharged or were they provided with proper service? It is not enough for the business of the festival to increase, its benefits must also be shared fairly among all those who produce, transport, sell, and buy. It would be good if the Nepal Rastra Bank, the National Statistics Office, customs, the tourism sector, and private entrepreneurs could work together to study the actual economic impact of Dashain. Questions such as how many goats were sold, how much remittances came in, how many people traveled, how much money went into domestic production, how much was spent on imports, and how many jobs were created need answers. Finally, I remember my father again. He sold two goats and got 80 thousand rupees. I exchanged 40 thousand rupees for it. But what was bigger than that 120 thousand rupees was one of his words, 'Kanchha, come this Dashain.' That one sentence brought me home. How many Nepalis return to such a call, how many cannot return and only send money? The economy of Dashain is based on this human connection. It connects the farmer's barn, the laborer's wages, the driver's steering wheel, the merchant's shop, and the savings of children earning abroad, all in one way or another. Dashain is not only a cultural identity of Nepal, but also one of the major seasonal backbones that drives currency flow, consumption, trade, employment, and rural-urban relations. The question of how much we spent is more important than how much Nepalis that spending brought income into the hands of.

ठाउँमा पुग्यो ! खसी गाउँबाट काठमाडौँ आएको भए अझ धेरै हात जोडिन्थे। किसान, सङ्कलनकर्ता, ट्रक चालक, सहचालक, बजारका मजदुर, मासु पसले र अन्तिम उपभोक्ता । किसानले ३० हजारमा बेचेको खसी सहरमा ४० हजारमा बिक्री भयो भने बीचको १० हजार सबै व्यापारीको नाफा होइन, ढुवानी, मजदुरी, हेरचाह र जोखिमको खर्च पनि त्यहीँबाट जान्छ । पशु सेवा क्षेत्रका अधिकारीलाई उद्धृत गरिएका सार्वजनिक विवरणमा दसैँका बेला देशभर करिब १० लाख खसी बोका बिक्री हुने अनुमान उल्लेख भएको छ। यसलाई औसत प्रतिगोटा २५ हजारदेखि ४० हजार रुपैयाँको मूल्यमा राखेर हेर्दा २५ देखि ४० अर्ब रुपैयाँको सम्भावित कारोबार देखिन्छ । यो बिक्रीको अन्तिम सरकारी हिसाब होइन, बजारको परिमाण बुझाउने अनुमान हो । काठमाडौँ उपत्यकामा मात्रै विभिन्न वर्षमा दसैँको आसपास दशौं हजार खसी बोका र च्याङ्ग्रा भित्रिएका विवरण छन् । मुस्ताङको च्याङ्ग्रा, कर्णालीको खसी, तराईको माछा र गाउँघरका कुखुरासम्म यसै मौसममा बजार पाउँछन् । दसैँमा खसी मात्र बिक्री हुँदैन । चामल, चिउरा, तेल, मसला, तरकारी, फलफूल, मिठाई, दूध र पेय पदार्थको माग बढ्छ । कसैले आफ्नै घरको खसी काट्छ, कसैले छिमेकीसँग मिलेर किन्छ । गाउँको पैसा गाउँमै अर्को घरमा पुग्छ । उधारो उठ्छ, बाँकी ज्याला तिरिन्छ, पसलमा रोकिएको हिसाब मिल्छ । बैंकको डिजिटल कारोबारमा नदेखिएका यस्ता साना नगद लेनदेन पनि आर्थिक जीवनका वास्तविक गतिविधि हुन् । गाउँको एउटा सानो बजार सम्झौँ । दसैँको अघिल्लो दिन किसानले खसी बेचेर ३५ हजार रुपैयाँ ल्यायो। उसले किराना पसलको पुरानो उधारो तिर्‍यो । किराना पसलेले थोक व्यापारीलाई बाँकी रकम बुझायो । त्यही पसलमा काम गर्ने युवाले पारिश्रमिक पाएपछि घरमा चामल र नयाँ कपडा लगे। उता खसी किनेको परिवारले मासु काट्ने व्यक्तिलाई ज्याला दियो, मसला र तरकारी किन्यो। यहाँ रकमको प्रत्येक हस्तान्तरण नयाँ आम्दानी होइन । तर एक अर्कासँग गाँसिएका धेरै परिवारको दैनिक जीवनलाई यसले सहज बनायो । नयाँ लुगा लगाउने परम्पराले कपडा, जुत्ता, सिलाइ, झोला, गहना र घरायसी सामानको बजार चलाउँछ । एउटा परिवारले पाँच जनाका लागि कपडा किन्दा त्यसको प्रभाव पसलदेखि थोक व्यापारी र ढुवानीसम्म पुग्छ। सामान चीन वा भारतबाट आएको रहेछ भने रकमको एउटा हिस्सा विदेशी उत्पादकसम्म पुग्छ । सन् २०२५ मा चाडपर्व लक्षित करिब ३५ अर्ब रुपैयाँ मूल्यका आयातित सामान सीमा अवरोधमा रोकिएको व्यापारीहरूको विवरणले पनि दसैँको बजार अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय आपूर्ति शृङ्खलासँग जोडिएको देखाउँछ । नेपाली ढाका, अल्लो, गार्मेन्ट, जुत्ता र घरेलु उत्पादनको हिस्सा बढाउन सके यही मागले देशभित्र थप रोजगारी दिन सक्छ । यातायातलाई हेरौँ । काठमाडौँमा काम गर्ने मानिस रोल्पा फर्किन्छ, पोखराको विद्यार्थी झापा जान्छ, विदेशबाट आएको छोरा विमानस्थलबाट गाउँ पुग्छ । बस मालिकले भाडा पाउँछ; चालक, सहचालक, इन्धन पम्प, बाटोको चिया पसल, होटेल र मिस्त्रीको पनि काम बढ्छ । घर फर्किने मानिसले आमाबुबाका लागि उपहार, छोराछोरीका लागि कपडा र घरका लागि सामान लिएर जान्छ । सहरमा कमाएको पैसा गाउँतर्फ बग्छ। घर रङ्गरोगन गर्दा पेन्टर, सिकर्मी, हार्डवेयर पसल र मजदुरको आम्दानी जोडिन्छ । दसैँको यात्राले सहरमा मात्र होइन, बाटोछेउका बस्तीमा पनि कारोबार बढाउँछ । बिहानैदेखि चिया पकाउने होटेल, खाना खुवाउने भोजनालय, पेट्रोल पम्प, टायर मर्मत गर्ने ग्यारेज र साना फलफूल पसलले ग्राहक पाउँछन् । एउटा बसमा चढेका चालीस यात्रुले फरक फरक ठाउँमा गरेको सानो खर्च जोड्दा पनि धेरै परिवारसम्म पैसा पुग्छ । तर अत्यधिक भाडा, भिडभाड र सडक दुर्घटनाको जोखिम कम गर्नसके मात्र यस्तो आवागमन सुरक्षित र फलदायी हुन्छ । विदेशमा रहेका नेपालीका लागि दसैँको अर्को अर्थ छ । कोही बिदा मिलाएर फर्किन्छन्, कोही टिकट महँगो भएर वा काम छाड्न नसकेर आउँदैनन् । फर्किन नसक्नेले पनि घरमा पैसा पठाउँछन् । विदेशको कमाइ आमाको हातमा पुग्छ, त्यो पैसा गाउँको किराना पसल, किसान र यातायात व्यवसायीसम्म पुग्छ । नेपालमा आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ मा करिब २३ खर्ब ६३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ रेमिटेन्स भित्रिएको प्रकाशित तथ्याङ्क छ। यसको मासिक औसत झन्डै १ खर्ब ९७ अर्ब हुन्छ। त्यो सबै दसैँमा खर्च हुने होइन, तर चाडपर्वको पारिवारिक खर्च धान्ने एउटा महत्त्वपूर्ण स्रोत रेमिटेन्स हो । विदेशबाट दसैँ मनाउन आउने मानिसको खर्चमा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय हवाई टिकट पनि जोडिन्छ । केही रकम विदेशी विमान कम्पनी र सेवा प्रदायककहाँ पुग्छ, केही नेपालका विमानस्थल, यातायात, होटेल र स्थानीय व्यवसायमा खर्च हुन्छ । फर्किन नसकेका नेपालीले घरमा पठाएको रकमले पनि बजार चलाउँछ । नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकको २०८२/८३ को वार्षिक विवरणअनुसार रेमिटेन्स करिब २३ खर्ब ६३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ पुगेको थियो। यो वर्षभरि आएको रकम हो, दसैँमा मात्रै आएको होइन। तथापि चाडपर्वको बेला विदेशको कमाइले परिवारको खर्च धान्न गर्ने सहयोगलाई यो परिमाणले बुझ्न मद्दत गर्छ । सरकारी र निजी क्षेत्रका धेरै कर्मचारीले दसैँको आसपास चाडपर्व खर्च पाउँछन् । श्रम ऐनले श्रमिकका लागि वर्षमा एक पटक एक महिनाको आधारभूत पारिश्रमिक बराबर चाडपर्व खर्चको व्यवस्था गरेको छ । मानौँ, १० लाख कर्मचारीले औसत ३० हजार रुपैयाँ पाए भने एकै अवधिमा ३० अर्ब रुपैयाँ उनीहरूको हातमा पुग्छ । यो उदाहरणका लागि गरिएको गणना हो। कसैले लुगा किन्छ, कसैले टिकट काट्छ, कसैले उधारो तिर्छ । व्यवसायका लागि भने तलब र चाडपर्व खर्च एकै पटक व्यवस्थापन गर्नुपर्ने दबाब पनि हुन्छ । राष्ट्रिय जनगणना २०७८ अनुसार नेपालमा ६६ लाख ६६ हजार ९३७ घरपरिवार छन् । सबैले दसैँ मनाउँदैनन् र खर्च पनि समान हुँदैन। तैपनि प्रतिपरिवार औसत २० हजार रुपैयाँ खर्च भएको परिकल्पना गर्दा करिब १ खर्ब ३३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ हुन्छ । औसत ३० हजार भए करिब दुई खर्ब रुपैयाँ पुग्छ । यो दसैँको प्रमाणित कुल खर्च होइन, यसको सम्भावित आर्थिक आकार बुझाउने हिसाब हो। खसी बोका, कपडा र यातायातका छुट्टाछुट्टै रकम यसमा फेरि जोड्दा एउटै खर्च दोहोरिन सक्ने भएकाले सावधानी चाहिन्छ । दसैँमा बैंकमा पैसा जम्मा हुन्छ, खाताबाट नगद निकालिन्छ, मोबाइल र QR बाट भुक्तानी हुन्छ । तर गाउँघरमा खसी किनबेच, मजदुरी, उधारो फर्छ्योट र साना पसलका धेरै कारोबार नगदमै पनि हुन्छन् । बैंकमा जम्मा भएको वा डिजिटल माध्यमबाट गएको रकमले मात्रै आर्थिक गतिविधिको सम्पूर्ण तस्बिर दिँदैन । मानौँ, किसानले ५० हजारको खसी बेच्यो, २० हजारको लुगा र खाद्यान्न किन्यो, पसलेले कर्मचारीलाई तलब दियो, कर्मचारीले घर भाडा तिर्‍यो । एउटै पैसा विभिन्न हातमा पुग्यो । यसलाई मुद्राको चलन गतिसँग जोडेर बुझ्न सकिन्छ । तर पटक पटक भएको कारोबारलाई त्यति नै नयाँ राष्ट्रिय आय भनेर गन्न मिल्दैन । बैंकको खातामा देखिएको कारोबार र गाउँको हाताहाती नगद कारोबारलाई एउटै कुरा ठान्न हुँदैन । उदाहरणका लागि, आमाले घरमा राखेको बचतबाट नातिलाई दक्षिणा दिनुभयो, नातिले पुस्तक वा जुत्ता किन्यो र पसलेले आपूर्तिकर्तालाई भुक्तानी गर्‍यो । यसमध्ये केही कारोबार बैंकको अभिलेखमा तुरुन्त नदेखिए पनि वस्तु र सेवाको वास्तविक कारोबार भएको हुन्छ । त्यसैले दसैँको आर्थिक आकार नाप्दा नगद, डिजिटल भुक्तानी, बचत, उधारो र वस्तुको आफ्नै घरमा हुने उपभोगसमेत बुझ्नुपर्छ । भारतमा दीपावली, चीनमा नयाँ वर्ष, अमेरिकामा क्रिसमसको किनमेल सिजन र मुस्लिम बहुल देशहरूमा ईदले पनि यात्रा, व्यापार, होटेल, उपहार र सेवा क्षेत्रलाई चलायमान बनाउँछन् । भारतको व्यापारी सङ्गठनले सन् २०२५ को दीपावली सिजनमा वस्तु र सेवातर्फ करिब ६.०५ लाख करोड भारतीय रुपैयाँको कारोबार भएको अनुमान सार्वजनिक गरेको थियो । खेलकुदतर्फ विश्वकप फुटबल र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय क्रिकेट प्रतियोगिताले पर्यटन, प्रसारण, विज्ञापन र आतिथ्य क्षेत्रमा यस्तै माग सिर्जना गर्छन् । नेपालमा दसैँसँगै तिहार, छठ, ल्होसार, माघी, इन्द्रजात्रा र अन्य पर्वहरूको पनि आर्थिक प्रभाव अध्ययन गर्न सकिन्छ । यद्यपि दसैँ सबैका लागि सहज हुँदैन । कसैले व्यापार बढाउँछ, कसैले ऋण लिएर चाडपर्व मनाउँछ । महङ्गो टिकट, बढ्दो मूल्य र सामाजिक अपेक्षाले कम आम्दानी भएका परिवारलाई दबाब दिन्छ । त्यसैले दसैँको आर्थिक सफलता कति रकम खर्च भयो भन्नेमा मात्र होइन, त्यसले कति नेपाली किसान, श्रमिक र उद्यमीको आम्दानी बढायो भन्नेमा खोज्नुपर्छ । दसैँको व्यापार बढेको खबरसँगै अर्को प्रश्न पनि उठ्छ नाफा कसको हातमा पुग्यो ? मुस्ताङको पशु पालकले उचित मूल्य पाए कि पाएनन् ? कपडा पसलका कर्मचारीले समयमै तलब पाए कि पाएनन् ? यात्रुबाट बढी भाडा उठाइयो कि उचित सेवा दिइयो ? चाडपर्वको कारोबार बढ्नु मात्र पर्याप्त छैन, त्यसको लाभ उत्पादन गर्ने, बोक्ने, बेच्ने र किन्ने सबैबीच न्यायोचित रूपमा बाँडिनु पनि आवश्यक छ । नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंक, राष्ट्रिय तथ्याङ्क कार्यालय, भन्सार, पर्यटन क्षेत्र र निजी व्यवसायीले मिलेर दसैँको वास्तविक आर्थिक प्रभाव अध्ययन गर्न सके राम्रो हुन्थ्यो। कति खसी बोका बिक्री भए, कति रेमिटेन्स आयो, कति मानिसले यात्रा गरे, कति रकम स्वदेशी उत्पादनमा गयो, कति आयातमा खर्च भयो र कति रोजगारी सिर्जना भयो यस्ता प्रश्नको उत्तर चाहिन्छ । अन्त्यमा फेरि बुबाकै कुरा सम्झिन्छु। उहाँले दुई वटा खसी बेचेर ८० हजार रुपैयाँ पाउनुभयो । मैले ४० हजार रुपैयाँ साटेर ल्याएँ । तर त्यो एक लाख २० हजारको हिसाबभन्दा ठूलो कुरा उहाँको एउटा वाक्य थियो ‘कान्छा, यो दसैँमा त आइज है ।’ त्यही एउटा वाक्यले मलाई घर फर्कायो । कति नेपाली यस्तै बोलावटमा फर्किन्छन् होला, कति फर्किन नसकेर पैसा मात्र पठाउँछन् होला । दसैँको अर्थतन्त्र यही मानवीय सम्बन्धमा टिकेको छ । किसानको गोठ, मजदुरको ज्याला, चालकको स्टेयरिङ, व्यापारीको पसल र विदेशमा कमाउने छोराछोरीको बचत सबैलाई यसले कुनै न कुनै रूपमा जोड्छ । दसैँ नेपालको सांस्कृतिक पहिचान मात्र होइन, मुद्रा प्रवाह, उपभोग, व्यापार, रोजगारी र ग्रामीण–सहरी सम्बन्धलाई चलायमान बनाउने प्रमुख मौसमी मेरुदण्डमध्ये एक हो । हामीले कति खर्च गर्‍यौँ भन्दा पनि त्यो खर्चले कति नेपालीको हातमा आम्दानी पुर्‍यायो भन्ने प्रश्न महत्त्वपूर्ण छ ।

यसपालि दसैँ मनाउन म आफ्नो गाउँ गुल्मी आएको छु । संयोगले पाँच वर्षदेखि दसैँ मनाउन पाएको थिइनँ । अघिल्लो महिना मात्रै नेपाल आएर फर्किएको थिएँ । फेरि यति चाँडै आउने योजना थिएन। तर एक दिन बुबाको फोन आयो । म घरको जेठो छोरा हुँ, तैपनि बुबाले मायाले सधैँ ‘कान्छा’ भन्नुहुन्छ। फोनमा पनि उही आत्मीय स्वर सुनियो, ‘कान्छा, यो दसैँमा त आइज है। अनि सुन् न, आउँदा ४० हजार जति पैसा साटेर ल्याएस् है ।’

बुबाले त्यति भनेपछि मनले मानेन । टिकट काटेँ, पैसा साटेँ र दसैँ मनाउन गुल्मीको घर आएँ । घरमा अर्को कुरा थाहा भयो । बुबाले घरमै पालेका दुई वटा खसी प्रतिगोटा ४० हजार रुपैयाँका दरले बेच्नुभएछ । दुई वटा खसीबाट ८० हजार रुपैयाँ आयो । मैले ल्याएको ४० हजार जोड्दा एउटै परिवारसँग सम्बन्धित एक लाख २० हजार रुपैयाँको आर्थिक प्रवाह देखियो । त्यो सबै दसैँमा खर्च भएको रकम होइन, तर पैसा कसरी एक घरबाट अर्को घर र गाउँको बजारसम्म पुग्छ भन्ने उदाहरण हो । त्यसपछि सोचेँ दसैँमा हाम्रो घरमा मात्रै यति रकम चलायमान भयो भने देशभरिका लाखौँ घरमा कति रकम घुम्दो हो ?

दसैँ टीका, जमरा र पारिवारिक मिलनको पर्व हो । तर यसले गाउँको गोठ, बजारको पसल, यातायात, बैंक, उद्योग र विदेशमा कमाइरहेका नेपालीलाई एउटै आर्थिक सम्बन्धमा जोड्छ। यसलाई केवल खर्च गर्ने पर्व भनेर बुझ्दा यसको ठूलो आर्थिक पक्ष छुट्छ ।

बुबाले बेच्नुभएको ४० हजारको खसी कसैले किनेर घरमा लग्यो । आफन्त जम्मा भएर मासु खाए । त्यो रकम बुबाको हातमा आयो । उहाँले त्यही पैसाले नातिनातिनालाई लुगा किन्नुभयो भने कपडा पसलेको व्यापार बढ्यो । पसलेले थोक व्यापारीलाई पैसा तिर्‍यो । थोक व्यापारीले सामान ढुवानी गर्ने गाडीलाई भाडा दियो । चालकले घरमा खाद्यान्न किन्यो । बुबाले केही रकम बैंकमा राख्नुभयो भने त्यो निक्षेपमार्फत वित्तीय प्रणालीमा पनि परिचालन हुन सक्छ। एउटै खसीको पैसा कति ठाउँमा पुग्यो !

खसी गाउँबाट काठमाडौँ आएको भए अझ धेरै हात जोडिन्थे। किसान, सङ्कलनकर्ता, ट्रक चालक, सहचालक, बजारका मजदुर, मासु पसले र अन्तिम उपभोक्ता । किसानले ३० हजारमा बेचेको खसी सहरमा ४० हजारमा बिक्री भयो भने बीचको १० हजार सबै व्यापारीको नाफा होइन, ढुवानी, मजदुरी, हेरचाह र जोखिमको खर्च पनि त्यहीँबाट जान्छ ।

पशु सेवा क्षेत्रका अधिकारीलाई उद्धृत गरिएका सार्वजनिक विवरणमा दसैँका बेला देशभर करिब १० लाख खसी बोका बिक्री हुने अनुमान उल्लेख भएको छ। यसलाई औसत प्रतिगोटा २५ हजारदेखि ४० हजार रुपैयाँको मूल्यमा राखेर हेर्दा २५ देखि ४० अर्ब रुपैयाँको सम्भावित कारोबार देखिन्छ । यो बिक्रीको अन्तिम सरकारी हिसाब होइन, बजारको परिमाण बुझाउने अनुमान हो । काठमाडौँ उपत्यकामा मात्रै विभिन्न वर्षमा दसैँको आसपास दशौं हजार खसी बोका र च्याङ्ग्रा भित्रिएका विवरण छन् ।

मुस्ताङको च्याङ्ग्रा, कर्णालीको खसी, तराईको माछा र गाउँघरका कुखुरासम्म यसै मौसममा बजार पाउँछन् । दसैँमा खसी मात्र बिक्री हुँदैन । चामल, चिउरा, तेल, मसला, तरकारी, फलफूल, मिठाई, दूध र पेय पदार्थको माग बढ्छ । कसैले आफ्नै घरको खसी काट्छ, कसैले छिमेकीसँग मिलेर किन्छ । गाउँको पैसा गाउँमै अर्को घरमा पुग्छ । उधारो उठ्छ, बाँकी ज्याला तिरिन्छ, पसलमा रोकिएको हिसाब मिल्छ । बैंकको डिजिटल कारोबारमा नदेखिएका यस्ता साना नगद लेनदेन पनि आर्थिक जीवनका वास्तविक गतिविधि हुन् ।

गाउँको एउटा सानो बजार सम्झौँ । दसैँको अघिल्लो दिन किसानले खसी बेचेर ३५ हजार रुपैयाँ ल्यायो। उसले किराना पसलको पुरानो उधारो तिर्‍यो । किराना पसलेले थोक व्यापारीलाई बाँकी रकम बुझायो । त्यही पसलमा काम गर्ने युवाले पारिश्रमिक पाएपछि घरमा चामल र नयाँ कपडा लगे। उता खसी किनेको परिवारले मासु काट्ने व्यक्तिलाई ज्याला दियो, मसला र तरकारी किन्यो। यहाँ रकमको प्रत्येक हस्तान्तरण नयाँ आम्दानी होइन । तर एक अर्कासँग गाँसिएका धेरै परिवारको दैनिक जीवनलाई यसले सहज बनायो ।

नयाँ लुगा लगाउने परम्पराले कपडा, जुत्ता, सिलाइ, झोला, गहना र घरायसी सामानको बजार चलाउँछ । एउटा परिवारले पाँच जनाका लागि कपडा किन्दा त्यसको प्रभाव पसलदेखि थोक व्यापारी र ढुवानीसम्म पुग्छ। सामान चीन वा भारतबाट आएको रहेछ भने रकमको एउटा हिस्सा विदेशी उत्पादकसम्म पुग्छ । सन् २०२५ मा चाडपर्व लक्षित करिब ३५ अर्ब रुपैयाँ मूल्यका आयातित सामान सीमा अवरोधमा रोकिएको व्यापारीहरूको विवरणले पनि दसैँको बजार अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय आपूर्ति शृङ्खलासँग जोडिएको देखाउँछ । नेपाली ढाका, अल्लो, गार्मेन्ट, जुत्ता र घरेलु उत्पादनको हिस्सा बढाउन सके यही मागले देशभित्र थप रोजगारी दिन सक्छ ।

यातायातलाई हेरौँ । काठमाडौँमा काम गर्ने मानिस रोल्पा फर्किन्छ, पोखराको विद्यार्थी झापा जान्छ, विदेशबाट आएको छोरा विमानस्थलबाट गाउँ पुग्छ । बस मालिकले भाडा पाउँछ; चालक, सहचालक, इन्धन पम्प, बाटोको चिया पसल, होटेल र मिस्त्रीको पनि काम बढ्छ । घर फर्किने मानिसले आमाबुबाका लागि उपहार, छोराछोरीका लागि कपडा र घरका लागि सामान लिएर जान्छ । सहरमा कमाएको पैसा गाउँतर्फ बग्छ। घर रङ्गरोगन गर्दा पेन्टर, सिकर्मी, हार्डवेयर पसल र मजदुरको आम्दानी जोडिन्छ ।

दसैँको यात्राले सहरमा मात्र होइन, बाटोछेउका बस्तीमा पनि कारोबार बढाउँछ । बिहानैदेखि चिया पकाउने होटेल, खाना खुवाउने भोजनालय, पेट्रोल पम्प, टायर मर्मत गर्ने ग्यारेज र साना फलफूल पसलले ग्राहक पाउँछन् । एउटा बसमा चढेका चालीस यात्रुले फरक फरक ठाउँमा गरेको सानो खर्च जोड्दा पनि धेरै परिवारसम्म पैसा पुग्छ । तर अत्यधिक भाडा, भिडभाड र सडक दुर्घटनाको जोखिम कम गर्नसके मात्र यस्तो आवागमन सुरक्षित र फलदायी हुन्छ ।

विदेशमा रहेका नेपालीका लागि दसैँको अर्को अर्थ छ । कोही बिदा मिलाएर फर्किन्छन्, कोही टिकट महँगो भएर वा काम छाड्न नसकेर आउँदैनन् । फर्किन नसक्नेले पनि घरमा पैसा पठाउँछन् । विदेशको कमाइ आमाको हातमा पुग्छ, त्यो पैसा गाउँको किराना पसल, किसान र यातायात व्यवसायीसम्म पुग्छ । नेपालमा आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ मा करिब २३ खर्ब ६३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ रेमिटेन्स भित्रिएको प्रकाशित तथ्याङ्क छ। यसको मासिक औसत झन्डै १ खर्ब ९७ अर्ब हुन्छ। त्यो सबै दसैँमा खर्च हुने होइन, तर चाडपर्वको पारिवारिक खर्च धान्ने एउटा महत्त्वपूर्ण स्रोत रेमिटेन्स हो ।

विदेशबाट दसैँ मनाउन आउने मानिसको खर्चमा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय हवाई टिकट पनि जोडिन्छ । केही रकम विदेशी विमान कम्पनी र सेवा प्रदायककहाँ पुग्छ, केही नेपालका विमानस्थल, यातायात, होटेल र स्थानीय व्यवसायमा खर्च हुन्छ । फर्किन नसकेका नेपालीले घरमा पठाएको रकमले पनि बजार चलाउँछ । नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकको २०८२/८३ को वार्षिक विवरणअनुसार रेमिटेन्स करिब २३ खर्ब ६३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ पुगेको थियो। यो वर्षभरि आएको रकम हो, दसैँमा मात्रै आएको होइन। तथापि चाडपर्वको बेला विदेशको कमाइले परिवारको खर्च धान्न गर्ने सहयोगलाई यो परिमाणले बुझ्न मद्दत गर्छ ।

सरकारी र निजी क्षेत्रका धेरै कर्मचारीले दसैँको आसपास चाडपर्व खर्च पाउँछन् । श्रम ऐनले श्रमिकका लागि वर्षमा एक पटक एक महिनाको आधारभूत पारिश्रमिक बराबर चाडपर्व खर्चको व्यवस्था गरेको छ । मानौँ, १० लाख कर्मचारीले औसत ३० हजार रुपैयाँ पाए भने एकै अवधिमा ३० अर्ब रुपैयाँ उनीहरूको हातमा पुग्छ । यो उदाहरणका लागि गरिएको गणना हो। कसैले लुगा किन्छ, कसैले टिकट काट्छ, कसैले उधारो तिर्छ । व्यवसायका लागि भने तलब र चाडपर्व खर्च एकै पटक व्यवस्थापन गर्नुपर्ने दबाब पनि हुन्छ ।

राष्ट्रिय जनगणना २०७८ अनुसार नेपालमा ६६ लाख ६६ हजार ९३७ घरपरिवार छन् । सबैले दसैँ मनाउँदैनन् र खर्च पनि समान हुँदैन। तैपनि प्रतिपरिवार औसत २० हजार रुपैयाँ खर्च भएको परिकल्पना गर्दा करिब १ खर्ब ३३ अर्ब रुपैयाँ हुन्छ । औसत ३० हजार भए करिब दुई खर्ब रुपैयाँ पुग्छ । यो दसैँको प्रमाणित कुल खर्च होइन, यसको सम्भावित आर्थिक आकार बुझाउने हिसाब हो। खसी बोका, कपडा र यातायातका छुट्टाछुट्टै रकम यसमा फेरि जोड्दा एउटै खर्च दोहोरिन सक्ने भएकाले सावधानी चाहिन्छ ।

दसैँमा बैंकमा पैसा जम्मा हुन्छ, खाताबाट नगद निकालिन्छ, मोबाइल र QR बाट भुक्तानी हुन्छ । तर गाउँघरमा खसी किनबेच, मजदुरी, उधारो फर्छ्योट र साना पसलका धेरै कारोबार नगदमै पनि हुन्छन् । बैंकमा जम्मा भएको वा डिजिटल माध्यमबाट गएको रकमले मात्रै आर्थिक गतिविधिको सम्पूर्ण तस्बिर दिँदैन । मानौँ, किसानले ५० हजारको खसी बेच्यो, २० हजारको लुगा र खाद्यान्न किन्यो, पसलेले कर्मचारीलाई तलब दियो, कर्मचारीले घर भाडा तिर्‍यो । एउटै पैसा विभिन्न हातमा पुग्यो । यसलाई मुद्राको चलन गतिसँग जोडेर बुझ्न सकिन्छ । तर पटक पटक भएको कारोबारलाई त्यति नै नयाँ राष्ट्रिय आय भनेर गन्न मिल्दैन ।

बैंकको खातामा देखिएको कारोबार र गाउँको हाताहाती नगद कारोबारलाई एउटै कुरा ठान्न हुँदैन । उदाहरणका लागि, आमाले घरमा राखेको बचतबाट नातिलाई दक्षिणा दिनुभयो, नातिले पुस्तक वा जुत्ता किन्यो र पसलेले आपूर्तिकर्तालाई भुक्तानी गर्‍यो । यसमध्ये केही कारोबार बैंकको अभिलेखमा तुरुन्त नदेखिए पनि वस्तु र सेवाको वास्तविक कारोबार भएको हुन्छ । त्यसैले दसैँको आर्थिक आकार नाप्दा नगद, डिजिटल भुक्तानी, बचत, उधारो र वस्तुको आफ्नै घरमा हुने उपभोगसमेत बुझ्नुपर्छ ।

भारतमा दीपावली, चीनमा नयाँ वर्ष, अमेरिकामा क्रिसमसको किनमेल सिजन र मुस्लिम बहुल देशहरूमा ईदले पनि यात्रा, व्यापार, होटेल, उपहार र सेवा क्षेत्रलाई चलायमान बनाउँछन् । भारतको व्यापारी सङ्गठनले सन् २०२५ को दीपावली सिजनमा वस्तु र सेवातर्फ करिब ६.०५ लाख करोड भारतीय रुपैयाँको कारोबार भएको अनुमान सार्वजनिक गरेको थियो । खेलकुदतर्फ विश्वकप फुटबल र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय क्रिकेट प्रतियोगिताले पर्यटन, प्रसारण, विज्ञापन र आतिथ्य क्षेत्रमा यस्तै माग सिर्जना गर्छन् । नेपालमा दसैँसँगै तिहार, छठ, ल्होसार, माघी, इन्द्रजात्रा र अन्य पर्वहरूको पनि आर्थिक प्रभाव अध्ययन गर्न सकिन्छ ।

यद्यपि दसैँ सबैका लागि सहज हुँदैन । कसैले व्यापार बढाउँछ, कसैले ऋण लिएर चाडपर्व मनाउँछ । महङ्गो टिकट, बढ्दो मूल्य र सामाजिक अपेक्षाले कम आम्दानी भएका परिवारलाई दबाब दिन्छ । त्यसैले दसैँको आर्थिक सफलता कति रकम खर्च भयो भन्नेमा मात्र होइन, त्यसले कति नेपाली किसान, श्रमिक र उद्यमीको आम्दानी बढायो भन्नेमा खोज्नुपर्छ ।

दसैँको व्यापार बढेको खबरसँगै अर्को प्रश्न पनि उठ्छ नाफा कसको हातमा पुग्यो ? मुस्ताङको पशु पालकले उचित मूल्य पाए कि पाएनन् ? कपडा पसलका कर्मचारीले समयमै तलब पाए कि पाएनन् ? यात्रुबाट बढी भाडा उठाइयो कि उचित सेवा दिइयो ? चाडपर्वको कारोबार बढ्नु मात्र पर्याप्त छैन, त्यसको लाभ उत्पादन गर्ने, बोक्ने, बेच्ने र किन्ने सबैबीच न्यायोचित रूपमा बाँडिनु पनि आवश्यक छ ।

नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंक, राष्ट्रिय तथ्याङ्क कार्यालय, भन्सार, पर्यटन क्षेत्र र निजी व्यवसायीले मिलेर दसैँको वास्तविक आर्थिक प्रभाव अध्ययन गर्न सके राम्रो हुन्थ्यो। कति खसी बोका बिक्री भए, कति रेमिटेन्स आयो, कति मानिसले यात्रा गरे, कति रकम स्वदेशी उत्पादनमा गयो, कति आयातमा खर्च भयो र कति रोजगारी सिर्जना भयो यस्ता प्रश्नको उत्तर चाहिन्छ ।

अन्त्यमा फेरि बुबाकै कुरा सम्झिन्छु। उहाँले दुई वटा खसी बेचेर ८० हजार रुपैयाँ पाउनुभयो । मैले ४० हजार रुपैयाँ साटेर ल्याएँ । तर त्यो एक लाख २० हजारको हिसाबभन्दा ठूलो कुरा उहाँको एउटा वाक्य थियो ‘कान्छा, यो दसैँमा त आइज है ।’ त्यही एउटा वाक्यले मलाई घर फर्कायो । कति नेपाली यस्तै बोलावटमा फर्किन्छन् होला, कति फर्किन नसकेर पैसा मात्र पठाउँछन् होला । दसैँको अर्थतन्त्र यही मानवीय सम्बन्धमा टिकेको छ । किसानको गोठ, मजदुरको ज्याला, चालकको स्टेयरिङ, व्यापारीको पसल र विदेशमा कमाउने छोराछोरीको बचत सबैलाई यसले कुनै न कुनै रूपमा जोड्छ ।

दसैँ नेपालको सांस्कृतिक पहिचान मात्र होइन, मुद्रा प्रवाह, उपभोग, व्यापार, रोजगारी र ग्रामीण–सहरी सम्बन्धलाई चलायमान बनाउने प्रमुख मौसमी मेरुदण्डमध्ये एक हो । हामीले कति खर्च गर्‍यौँ भन्दा पनि त्यो खर्चले कति नेपालीको हातमा आम्दानी पुर्‍यायो भन्ने प्रश्न महत्त्वपूर्ण छ ।

This time, I have come to my village Gulmi to celebrate Dashain. Coincidentally, I had not been able to celebrate Dashain for five years. I had only returned from Nepal last month. I had not planned to come back so soon. But one day, my father called me. I am the eldest son of the family, yet my father always affectionately calls me 'Kancha'. The same affectionate voice was heard on the phone, 'Kancha, come this Dashain. And listen, when you came, you brought 40,000 rupees in exchange.' When my father said that, I didn't agree. I bought a ticket, exchanged money, and came home to Gulmi to celebrate Dashain. I learned something else at home. My father had sold two goats he had raised at home for 40,000 rupees each. He earned 80,000 rupees from the two goats. When I added the 40,000 I brought, I saw a financial flow of 120,000 rupees belonging to the same family. That's not all the money spent on Dashain, but it's an example of how money reaches from one house to another and to the village market. Then I thought, if this much money circulates in our house alone during Dashain, how much money circulates in millions of homes across the country? Dashain is a festival of tika, jamara, and family reunions. But it also connects the village cowshed, market shops, transportation, banks, industries, and Nepalis earning abroad into a single economic relationship. Understanding it as a festival of spending only misses its huge economic aspect. Someone bought the goat that the father had sold for 40,000 and took it home. The relatives gathered and ate the meat. That money came into the father's hands. He used the same money to buy clothes for his grandchildren, and the business of the cloth shop grew. The shopkeeper paid the money to the wholesaler. The wholesaler rented a vehicle to transport the goods. The driver bought food for the house. If the father had put some money in the bank, that money could also be mobilized in the financial system through deposits. How many places could the money from a single goat have reached! If the goat had come from the village to Kathmandu, more hands would have been joined. Farmers, collectors, truck drivers, assistant drivers, market workers, butchers, and the final consumer. If a goat sold by a farmer for 30,000 is sold in the city for 40,000, the 10,000 in between is not only the profit of the trader, but also the cost of transportation, labor, care, and risk. Public statements quoted from livestock service officials indicate that around one million goats and sheep will be sold across the country during Dashain. If we put this at an average price of Rs 25,000 to Rs 40,000 per goat, a potential turnover of Rs 25 to 40 billion is seen. This is not the final government estimate of sales, but an estimate to indicate the size of the market. In the Kathmandu Valley alone, there are reports of tens of thousands of goats and sheep being imported around Dashain in various years. Mustang's Chyangra, Karnali's Khasi, Terai fish, and even village chickens find a market during this season. Not only is Khasi sold during Dashain. Demand for rice, Chiura, oil, spices, vegetables, fruits, sweets, milk, and beverages increases. Some slaughter their own goats, while others buy them together with their neighbors. Village money reaches other households in the village. Loans are taken out, wages are paid, and accounts held in shops are settled. Such small cash transactions that are not visible in the bank's digital transactions are also real activities of economic life. Let's think of a small market in the village. The day before Dashain, a farmer sold a goat and brought 35,000 rupees. He paid off the old loan from the grocery store. The grocery store paid the remaining amount to the wholesaler. After receiving his salary, the young man working in the same store took home rice and new clothes. On the other hand, the family that bought the goat paid the wages of the butcher, bought spices and vegetables. Here, each transfer of money is not new income. But it has made the daily life of many families who are closely connected to each other easier. The tradition of wearing new clothes drives the market for clothes, shoes, sewing, bags, jewelry, and household goods. When a family of five buys clothes, the impact extends from the store to the wholesaler and the transporter. If the goods come from China or India, a portion of the money goes to the foreign manufacturer. Traders’ accounts of about Rs 35 billion worth of imported goods targeted for the festival in 2025 being stopped at border barriers also show that the Dashain market is linked to the international supply chain. If the share of Nepali Dhaka, Allo, Garment, Shoes, and Home Products can be increased, this demand could create more jobs within the country. Let's look at transportation. A person working in Kathmandu returns to Rolpa, a student from Pokhara goes to Jhapa, a son who has come from abroad reaches his village from the airport. The bus owner gets the fare; the work of the driver, co-driver, fuel pump, roadside tea shop, hotel and mechanic also increases. People returning home take gifts for their parents, clothes for their children and household goods. The money earned in the city flows to the village. When a house is painted, the income of the painter, carpenter, hardware shop and laborer increases. Dashain travel not only increases business in the city but also in the roadside settlements. Hotels serving tea, restaurants serving food, petrol pumps, tire repair garages and small fruit shops get customers from the morning. Even if the small expenses of forty passengers on a bus are added up, the money reaches many families. But such travel is safe and fruitful only if the risk of high fares, congestion and road accidents can be reduced. For Nepalis living abroad, Dashain has another meaning. Some return after arranging a vacation, some do not come because the ticket is expensive or they cannot leave work. Even those who cannot return send money home. The earnings from abroad reach the hands of their mothers, and that money reaches the village grocery stores, farmers, and transport entrepreneurs. There is published data that about 2.363 trillion rupees in remittances entered Nepal in the fiscal year 2082/83. Its monthly average is about 1.97 trillion. Not all of that is spent on Dashain, but remittances are an important source of meeting family expenses during the festival. International airfares are also part of the expenses of people coming from abroad to celebrate Dashain. Some of the money goes to foreign airlines and service providers, while some is spent on Nepali airports, transportation, hotels, and local businesses. The market is also driven by the money sent home by Nepalis who are unable to return. According to the annual report of Nepal Rastra Bank for 2082/83, remittances reached about 2.363 trillion rupees. This is the amount received throughout the year, not just during Dashain. However, this amount helps to understand the contribution of foreign earnings to meet family expenses during the festival. Many government and private sector employees receive festive expenses around Dashain. The Labor Act has made a provision for festive expenses equal to one month's basic salary for workers once a year. Suppose, if one million employees receive an average of 30 thousand rupees, 30 billion rupees will reach their hands in the same period. This is a calculation done for example. Some buy clothes, some buy tickets, some pay off loans. For businesses, there is also pressure to manage salaries and festive expenses at the same time. According to the National Census 2078, there are 66,66,937 households in Nepal. Not everyone celebrates Dashain and the expenses are not the same. However, assuming an average expenditure of Rs 20,000 per household, it is about Rs 133 billion. If the average is Rs 30,000, it is about Rs 200 billion. This is not the verified total expenditure of Dashain, but an estimate of its potential economic size. Caution is required as the same expenditure may be repeated when separate amounts for goats, clothes and transportation are added to this. During Dashain, money is deposited in banks, cash is withdrawn from accounts, and payments are made through mobile and QR. But in rural areas, goat buying and selling, wages, loan repayments, and many small shop transactions are also done in cash. The amount deposited in banks or transferred through digital channels alone does not give the entire picture of economic activity. Suppose, a farmer sold a goat worth 50,000, bought clothes and food worth 20,000, a shopkeeper paid his employees' salaries, and an employee paid his house rent. The same money reached different hands. This can be understood by linking it to the movement of money. But repeated transactions cannot be counted as new national income. The transactions seen in the bank account and the cash transactions in the village should not be considered the same thing. For example, a mother gave dakshina to her grandson from the savings kept at home, the grandson bought books or shoes, and a shopkeeper paid a supplier. Some of these transactions, although not immediately visible in the bank's records, are actual transactions of goods and services. Therefore, when measuring the economic size of Dashain, cash, digital payments, savings, loans, and consumption of goods in one's own home should also be considered. Diwali in India, New Year in China, Christmas shopping season in the US and Eid in Muslim-majority countries also drive the travel, trade, hotel, gift and service sectors. The Confederation of Indian Industry had estimated that the turnover of goods and services during the Diwali season in 2025 was around 6.05 lakh crore Indian rupees. In sports, the World Cup football and international cricket tournaments create similar demand in the tourism, broadcasting, advertising and hospitality sectors. Along with Dashain in Nepal, the economic impact of Tihar, Chhath, Lhosar, Maghi, Indrajatra and other festivals can also be studied. However, Dashain is not easy for everyone. Some increase their business, some take out loans to celebrate the festival. Expensive tickets, rising prices, and social expectations put pressure on low-income families. Therefore, the economic success of Dashain should be seen not only in how much money was spent, but also in how many Nepali farmers, workers, and entrepreneurs it increased their income. With the news of increased Dashain business, another question arises: who gets the profit? Did the cattle breeders of Mustang get a fair price or not? Did the employees of the clothing store get their salaries on time or not? Were passengers overcharged or were they provided with proper service? It is not enough for the business of the festival to increase, its benefits must also be shared fairly among all those who produce, transport, sell, and buy. It would be good if the Nepal Rastra Bank, the National Statistics Office, customs, the tourism sector, and private entrepreneurs could work together to study the actual economic impact of Dashain. Questions such as how many goats were sold, how much remittances came in, how many people traveled, how much money went into domestic production, how much was spent on imports, and how many jobs were created need answers. Finally, I remember my father again. He sold two goats and got 80 thousand rupees. I exchanged 40 thousand rupees for it. But what was bigger than that 120 thousand rupees was one of his words, 'Kanchha, come this Dashain.' That one sentence brought me home. How many Nepalis return to such a call, how many cannot return and only send money? The economy of Dashain is based on this human connection. It connects the farmer's barn, the laborer's wages, the driver's steering wheel, the merchant's shop, and the savings of children earning abroad, all in one way or another. Dashain is not only a cultural identity of Nepal, but also one of the major seasonal backbones that drives currency flow, consumption, trade, employment, and rural-urban relations. The question of how much we spent is more important than how much Nepalis that spending brought income into the hands of.

When I added the 40,000 I brought, I saw a financial flow of 120,000 rupees belonging to the same family. That's not all the money spent on Dashain, but it's an example of how money reaches from one house to another and to the village market. Then I thought, if this much money circulates in our house alone during Dashain, how much money circulates in millions of homes across the country?

Dashain is a festival of tika, jamara, and family reunions. But it also connects the village cowshed, market shops, transportation, banks, industries, and Nepalis earning abroad into a single economic relationship. Understanding it as a festival of spending only misses its huge economic aspect.

Someone bought the goat that the father had sold for 40,000 and took it home. The relatives gathered and ate the meat. That money came into the father's hands. He used the same money to buy clothes for his grandchildren, and the business of the cloth shop grew. The shopkeeper paid the money to the wholesaler. The wholesaler rented a vehicle to transport the goods. The driver bought food for the house. If the father had put some money in the bank, that money could also be mobilized in the financial system through deposits. How many places could the money from a single goat have reached!

If the goat had come from the village to Kathmandu, more hands would have been joined. Farmers, collectors, truck drivers, assistant drivers, market workers, butchers, and the final consumer. If a goat sold by a farmer for 30,000 is sold in the city for 40,000, the 10,000 in between is not only the profit of the trader, but also the cost of transportation, labor, care, and risk.

Public statements quoted from livestock service officials indicate that around one million goats and sheep will be sold across the country during Dashain. If we put this at an average price of Rs 25,000 to Rs 40,000 per goat, a potential turnover of Rs 25 to 40 billion is seen. This is not the final government estimate of sales, but an estimate to indicate the size of the market. In the Kathmandu Valley alone, there are reports of tens of thousands of goats and sheep being imported around Dashain in various years.

Mustang's Chyangra, Karnali's Khasi, Terai fish, and even village chickens find a market during this season. Not only is Khasi sold during Dashain. Demand for rice, Chiura, oil, spices, vegetables, fruits, sweets, milk, and beverages increases. Some slaughter their own goats, while others buy them together with their neighbors. Village money reaches other households in the village. Loans are taken out, wages are paid, and accounts held in shops are settled. Such small cash transactions that are not visible in the bank's digital transactions are also real activities of economic life.

Let's think of a small market in the village. The day before Dashain, a farmer sold a goat and brought 35,000 rupees. He paid off the old loan from the grocery store. The grocery store paid the remaining amount to the wholesaler. After receiving his salary, the young man working in the same store took home rice and new clothes. On the other hand, the family that bought the goat paid the wages of the butcher, bought spices and vegetables. Here, each transfer of money is not new income. But it has made the daily life of many families who are closely connected to each other easier.

The tradition of wearing new clothes drives the market for clothes, shoes, sewing, bags, jewelry, and household goods. When a family of five buys clothes, the impact extends from the store to the wholesaler and the transporter. If the goods come from China or India, a portion of the money goes to the foreign manufacturer. Traders’ accounts of about Rs 35 billion worth of imported goods targeted for the festival in 2025 being stopped at border barriers also show that the Dashain market is linked to the international supply chain. If the share of Nepali Dhaka, Allo, Garment, Shoes, and Home Products can be increased, this demand could create more jobs within the country.

Let's look at transportation. A person working in Kathmandu returns to Rolpa, a student from Pokhara goes to Jhapa, a son who has come from abroad reaches his village from the airport. The bus owner gets the fare; the work of the driver, co-driver, fuel pump, roadside tea shop, hotel and mechanic also increases. People returning home take gifts for their parents, clothes for their children and household goods. The money earned in the city flows to the village. When a house is painted, the income of the painter, carpenter, hardware shop and laborer increases.

Dashain travel not only increases business in the city but also in the roadside settlements. Hotels serving tea, restaurants serving food, petrol pumps, tire repair garages and small fruit shops get customers from the morning. Even if the small expenses of forty passengers on a bus are added up, the money reaches many families. But such travel is safe and fruitful only if the risk of high fares, congestion and road accidents can be reduced.

For Nepalis living abroad, Dashain has another meaning. Some return after arranging a vacation, some do not come because the ticket is expensive or they cannot leave work. Even those who cannot return send money home. The earnings from abroad reach the hands of their mothers, and that money reaches the village grocery stores, farmers, and transport entrepreneurs. There is published data that about 2.363 trillion rupees in remittances entered Nepal in the fiscal year 2082/83. Its monthly average is about 1.97 trillion. Not all of that is spent on Dashain, but remittances are an important source of meeting family expenses during the festival.

International airfares are also part of the expenses of people coming from abroad to celebrate Dashain. Some of the money goes to foreign airlines and service providers, while some is spent on Nepali airports, transportation, hotels, and local businesses. The market is also driven by the money sent home by Nepalis who are unable to return. According to the annual report of Nepal Rastra Bank for 2082/83, remittances reached about 2.363 trillion rupees. This is the amount received throughout the year, not just during Dashain. However, this amount helps to understand the contribution of foreign earnings to meet family expenses during the festival.

Many government and private sector employees receive festive expenses around Dashain. The Labor Act has made a provision for festive expenses equal to one month's basic salary for workers once a year. Suppose, if one million employees receive an average of 30 thousand rupees, 30 billion rupees will reach their hands in the same period. This is a calculation done for example. Some buy clothes, some buy tickets, some pay off loans. For businesses, there is also pressure to manage salaries and festive expenses at the same time.

According to the National Census 2078, there are 66,66,937 households in Nepal. Not everyone celebrates Dashain and the expenses are not the same. However, assuming an average expenditure of Rs 20,000 per household, it is about Rs 133 billion. If the average is Rs 30,000, it is about Rs 200 billion. This is not the verified total expenditure of Dashain, but an estimate of its potential economic size. Caution is required as the same expenditure may be repeated when separate amounts for goats, clothes and transportation are added to this.

During Dashain, money is deposited in banks, cash is withdrawn from accounts, and payments are made through mobile and QR. But in rural areas, goat buying and selling, wages, loan repayments, and many small shop transactions are also done in cash. The amount deposited in banks or transferred through digital channels alone does not give the entire picture of economic activity. Suppose, a farmer sold a goat worth 50,000, bought clothes and food worth 20,000, a shopkeeper paid his employees' salaries, and an employee paid his house rent. The same money reached different hands. This can be understood by linking it to the movement of money. But repeated transactions cannot be counted as new national income.

The transactions seen in the bank account and the cash transactions in the village should not be considered the same thing. For example, a mother gave dakshina to her grandson from the savings kept at home, the grandson bought books or shoes, and a shopkeeper paid a supplier. Some of these transactions, although not immediately visible in the bank's records, are actual transactions of goods and services. Therefore, when measuring the economic size of Dashain, cash, digital payments, savings, loans, and consumption of goods in one's own home should also be considered.

Diwali in India, New Year in China, Christmas shopping season in the US and Eid in Muslim-majority countries also drive the travel, trade, hotel, gift and service sectors. The Confederation of Indian Industry had estimated that the turnover of goods and services during the Diwali season in 2025 was around 6.05 lakh crore Indian rupees. In sports, the World Cup football and international cricket tournaments create similar demand in the tourism, broadcasting, advertising and hospitality sectors. Along with Dashain in Nepal, the economic impact of Tihar, Chhath, Lhosar, Maghi, Indrajatra and other festivals can also be studied.

However, Dashain is not easy for everyone. Some increase their business, some take out loans to celebrate the festival. Expensive tickets, rising prices, and social expectations put pressure on low-income families. Therefore, the economic success of Dashain should be seen not only in how much money was spent, but also in how many Nepali farmers, workers, and entrepreneurs it increased their income.

With the news of increased Dashain business, another question arises: who gets the profit? Did the cattle breeders of Mustang get a fair price or not? Did the employees of the clothing store get their salaries on time or not? Were passengers overcharged or were they provided with proper service? It is not enough for the business of the festival to increase, its benefits must also be shared fairly among all those who produce, transport, sell, and buy.

It would be good if the Nepal Rastra Bank, the National Statistics Office, customs, the tourism sector, and private entrepreneurs could work together to study the actual economic impact of Dashain. Questions such as how many goats were sold, how much remittances came in, how many people traveled, how much money went into domestic production, how much was spent on imports, and how many jobs were created need answers.

Finally, I remember my father again. He sold two goats and got 80 thousand rupees. I exchanged 40 thousand rupees for it. But what was bigger than that 120 thousand rupees was one of his words, 'Kanchha, come this Dashain.' That one sentence brought me home. How many Nepalis return to such a call, how many cannot return and only send money? The economy of Dashain is based on this human connection. It connects the farmer's barn, the laborer's wages, the driver's steering wheel, the merchant's shop, and the savings of children earning abroad, all in one way or another.

Dashain is not only a cultural identity of Nepal, but also one of the major seasonal backbones that drives currency flow, consumption, trade, employment, and rural-urban relations. The question of how much we spent is more important than how much Nepalis that spending brought income into the hands of.
